opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about it as three goals that pull against each other, so a lot of the work is managing the trade-offs.

**Capability** comes first, because if the model can't produce physically plausible worlds, speed doesn't matter. For Cosmos, that starts with data. We spend a lot of effort curating video that's rich in physical interaction: objects moving, colliding, being manipulated, cameras moving through real spaces. Filtering, captioning, and deduplicating at scale is unglamorous, but in my experience it's often where the biggest gains come from. On the modeling side, we explore both diffusion-based and autoregressive approaches, because they have different strengths. Diffusion tends to give higher visual quality. Autoregressive models fit more naturally with how people think about language models and with real-time interaction.

**Generalization** is the real goal of a *foundation* model. We don't want something that only works on one robot or one driving setup. The bet is that if you pre-train on a broad, diverse distribution of the physical world, the model learns general priors: object permanence, how things fall, how light behaves. Then you post-train for a specific domain, like a particular robot arm or camera rig, with a relatively small amount of data. So we deliberately separate the general pre-training stage from domain-specific post-training, and we design the model so post-training is easy for developers to do themselves. We also lean on conditioning signals like depth, segmentation, and edges, so people can steer the model toward their scenario without retraining from scratch.

**Speed** matters because the main use cases are generating synthetic training data, evaluating policies, and eventually serving as a simulator in the loop, and all of those need a lot of generation. The tokenizer is a big lever. If you compress video into a compact latent space without losing the important details, everything downstream gets cheaper. Beyond that, we use distillation to cut the number of sampling steps, offer different model sizes so people can pick their point on the quality-speed curve, and, being at NVIDIA, co-design with the hardware and inference stack.

The way I tie it together: you push capability and generality with scale and data, then you claw back efficiency with better tokenizers, distillation, and systems work. And you keep checking against what physical AI developers actually need, because a world model is ultimately a tool for training and testing robots and autonomous vehicles. That feedback loop tells us which trade-offs are worth making.

r001.rationale: The response describes trade-offs, exploring two model approaches, and checking developer feedback, but it does not clearly frame how to improve capabilities and generalization as an empirical question that must be answered through experimentation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Let me take those three in turn, because for us they are really one problem viewed from different angles.

Start with generalization, since that drives everything else. Cosmos is a world foundation model, which means its job is to understand physics, space, time, and how objects interact, well enough to simulate what happens next in a scene. A model like that only becomes useful if it handles situations it never saw in training. So the first lever is data. We curated an enormous amount of video, on the order of tens of millions of hours, and we spent a lot of effort on filtering and annotation. It is not just scale. Video from a driving camera, a warehouse robot, a human doing a task, a first-person walkthrough, all of these teach the model different aspects of physical behavior. We built pipelines to caption that data, deduplicate it, and reject clips that are visually fine but physically uninformative. Diversity in the physical phenomena matters more than raw hours. We also found that pretraining broadly and then post-training for a specific embodiment, a particular robot or a particular car sensor rig, is a far better recipe than trying to train the specialized model from scratch. The base model carries the general physical prior, and the fine-tuning adapts it.

On capabilities, we deliberately released more than one architecture. There is a diffusion family and an autoregressive family. Diffusion gives you very high visual fidelity, which matters when you want to use the output as realistic synthetic data. Autoregressive models tokenize video and predict the next token, which makes them natural for planning and for interleaving with language and actions. Both have a place, and we wanted the community to be able to choose. We also built a tokenizer that compresses video far more aggressively than earlier ones while keeping quality, because every downstream model inherits the tokenizer's limits. Then there is control. A world model that only produces pretty video is not that useful to a roboticist. You need to condition on camera trajectory, on actions, on text, on segmentation or depth maps. Much of what we consider capability work is making the model controllable in the ways physical AI developers actually need.

Speed is where the engineering discipline comes in, and honestly it is where a lot of the research value gets realized or lost. If a robotics team wants to generate a million synthetic training clips, a model that takes minutes per clip is not a tool, it is a demo. So we attacked latency from several directions. Distillation, so a diffusion model that needed many sampling steps can produce comparable results in a handful. Better tokenizers, so there are simply fewer tokens to process. Inference optimizations from our platform side, quantization, kernel fusion, running efficiently across GPUs. And at the architecture level, thinking about which parts of the model need to run at full resolution and which can operate in a compressed latent space.

The thing I keep emphasizing to the team is that these are not in tension. Faster inference means we can run many more evaluations, which means we learn faster what generalizes and what does not. Better generalization means we need less bespoke fine-tuning per deployment, which effectively makes the whole system faster for the end user. And we tie all of it to concrete physical AI use cases, because that is the only honest test. A model can look wonderful on a benchmark and still produce a ball that falls the wrong way. We would rather be judged by whether a robot trained partly on our synthetic data actually works in a real warehouse.

r001.rationale: The response ties improvement to empirical evaluation: it says broader pretraining and embodiment-specific post-training were found to work better, and that faster inference enables more evaluations to reveal what generalizes. It also says physical AI use cases are the test.

astra-6.text:
I think about speed, capability, and generalization together, because improving one in isolation can create tradeoffs elsewhere. A faster model is useful only if it preserves the capabilities you need, and strong performance on familiar examples doesn’t necessarily mean it will work in a new environment.

My approach would be to start with the intended use case and define how to measure all three. Then I’d look at where the bottlenecks are: the data, the model architecture, the training process, or inference. For speed, you can explore more efficient computation or distillation, but you have to check what quality you lose. For capability and generalization, I would emphasize diverse training data and evaluation on situations that differ meaningfully from the training set.

The key is to make that an iterative process: change something, measure the gains and tradeoffs, and use the failures to guide the next experiment.

r001.rationale: The response says to evaluate capability and generalization on diverse, unfamiliar situations, then iteratively change something, measure gains and tradeoffs, and use failures to guide the next experiment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of speed, capability, and generalization as connected goals. For a world model like Cosmos, speed is valuable if the model still captures the dynamics that matter. So you have to ask: can we make it more efficient while preserving temporal consistency, physical plausibility, and controllability?

My approach is to start with the use case, identify the bottleneck, and then improve the data, the model, and the inference pipeline together. You might explore better representations, more efficient architectures, or distillation, but you need to evaluate what each change does to quality.

For generalization, the key is diversity in both training and evaluation. A model can produce impressive examples and still struggle with unfamiliar environments or interactions. So I would look beyond visual quality and test whether it behaves consistently in situations different from those it has seen. The goal is useful, reliable world simulation at a practical computational cost.

r001.rationale: The response says to explore possible improvements and evaluate their effects on quality, and to test generalization in unfamiliar situations. This clearly frames how to improve capabilities and generalization as something to determine empirically.
